newsitem.title: USA: Rivlin backs strong US economy with low inflation.
newsitem.headline: Rivlin backs strong US economy with low inflation.

text.p: Federal Reserve Board Vice Chair Alice Rivlin Friday backed the strongest possible growth for the U.S. economy as long as it didn't generate inflation.

Speaking to an economists group, Rivlin said she backed the dual Humphrey-Hawkins Fed mandate of fostering jobs growth and low inflation rather than requiring policymakers to only concentrate on inflation in setting policy.
"We ought to be on the highest growth track that is sustainable and to stay on it with as few ups and downs as possible," she said.

She said that low inflation should not be thought of as an end in itself and that it would be a mistake as some in Congress have suggested to give the Fed a single objective of reducing inflation on which to focus monetary policy.

"It would be especially unfortunate to specify a zero inflation target, first because we don't measure inflation well enough to know when we have hit an exact target, and second because the benefits of getting all the way to zero may not be all that great and the costs could be substantial."
In discussing the Fed's decision to raise rates last month, Rivlin said that it was done because of the perceived possibility of the U.S. economy overheating in months ahead.
Rivlin also said that current low U.S. inflation levels were due in part to the strength of the dollar.
"We're clearly benefitting on the inflation front from the fact that the dollar has moved up quite a lot and our growing imports are cheaper," she said.
She said that any inflation forecast had to take into account the likely level of the dollar, and said the U.S. economy was increasingly affected by the economies of the rest of the world.
She said the dollar was strong mainly because global investors saw the United States as a good place to put their money, rather than because of the level of U.S. interest rates.
"I think what's strengthening the dollar at the moment is the general good feeling that the rest of the world is having about the U.S. economy," she said.
"That may be somewhat increased by the doubts around the European (monetary union), whether it's going forward or not," she added.
